name: Fitzgerald Star Vibrator

card.summary: A 1920s electric hand-held massage vibrator advertised for face and body massage, with claims of firmer skin and muscle.
card.note: Historical item; claims came from period advertising.

quick.overview:
The Fitzgerald Star vibrator was an electric massage vibrator sold in the 1910s and 1920s, marketed through film and women's magazines. Advertising promoted it for face, hair and body massage, with claims about skin tone and muscle development.

It belongs to a wave of early home electrical appliances sold for health and beauty. Surviving examples are collected, and the device is documented as an electromagnet driven from mains power.
quick.how: Period ads described applying the vibrating tip to the face, scalp and body as a massage, with a free home trial offered by the maker. A 1919 ad listed the complete outfit at $5.
quick.risks: No modern assessment of its effects exists. Beauty claims in vibrator advertising of the period were not backed by controlled studies, and early electrical devices carried general electrical safety concerns.

lead: The Fitzgerald Star vibrator was an electric massage vibrator made by the Fitzgerald Mfg. Co. of Torrington, Connecticut, and advertised around 1919-1921 in film magazines [1]. A related patent, US 1327466 "Massage Vibrator" by P. J. Fitzgerald, was granted on 6 January 1920 [2].

Home vibrators were sold from about 1900 as electrical appliances for health and beauty, with advertisements promising relief from complaints from headaches to wrinkles and treatments for skin and scalp [3]. Fitzgerald advertising used celebrity testimonials and promoted the device for face, hair and body development, according to a dealer listing of a 1919 ad [1].
Technically, the device is described as an electromagnet powered from AC mains, vibrating at 60 Hz in the US, with a screw-in applicator tip [2]. No clinical research on the product exists.

chain: Vibrating tip applied to face or body
Advertised as stimulating circulation and toning skin and muscle
Claimed: firmer skin and body development
angle.text: Early advertising for the Star vibrator promoted facial and body massage for complexion and muscle development. These were period marketing claims.

paras: Electric vibrators began as medical instruments in the late 19th century, with Joseph Mortimer Granville's 1883 book describing uses such as neuralgia and indigestion [3]. By 1900 magazines advertised them for home use as health and beauty appliances, and mail order was the main sales route from 1900 to 1920 [3]. A 1899 ad promised a cure for "Neuralgia, Headache, Wrinkles" [3].
Fitzgerald ran ads in magazines in 1919-1920, including a January 1920 Cosmopolitan ad [1][2]. By the mid-1920s vibrators left respectable publications and ads nearly disappeared until the 1960s [3].

timeline.event: Star vibrator advertised with an actress testimonial.[1]
